etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Latin suffōcāre, from sub- (“under, up to”) + fōx (“throat”).

definitions.definition: (ergative) To suffer, or cause someone to suffer, from severely reduced oxygen intake to the body.

quote.citation: 2020 November 2, Jiu Xiao, “Chinese Communist Party Officials Push Anti-U.S. Propaganda While Sending Families to Live in the U.S.”, in Minghui‎[1]:
quote.text: It is because of freedom, one netizen replied: Like air, you may not realize its importance, but when suffocating, you would know how precious it is.

definitions.definition: (ergative) To die due to, or kill someone by means of, insufficient oxygen supply to the body.

quote.citation: 1599 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Life of Henry the Fift”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act III, scene vi]:
quote.text: Let not hemp his windpipe suffocate.

definitions.definition: (ergative, figuratively) To overwhelm, or be overwhelmed (by a person or issue), as though with oxygen deprivation.

quote.citation: 1962 April, “London Airport rail link”, in Modern Railways, page 222:
quote.text: If the trend to private cars continues, the more quickly will the road traffic suffocate itself, [...].

quote.citation: c. 1602, William Shakespeare, “The Tragedie of Troylus and Cressida”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act I, scene iii]:
quote.text: This chaos , when degree is suffocate , Follows the choking
